= GitHub Workflows — what runs, and why some look duplicated

This directory holds the repo's CI/CD. A few workflows *look* like they overlap
but are deliberately distinct — documented here so the apparent duplication is
not "tidied away" into a real coverage gap.

== Hypatia runs in two places (on purpose)

* `hypatia-scan.yml` — the **standalone security scan** (push / PR / weekly).
  Independent; this is the repo's own Hypatia coverage.
* `static-analysis-gate.yml` -> `hypatia-scan` job — runs Hypatia as part of the
  **gate**, then the `deposit-findings` job hands the results to the
  **gitbot-fleet learning** pipeline. This job is *documented here as a
  required status check*, but as of 2026-11-08 no live rule requires it:
  `GET /rules/branches/main` returns only `required_linear_history`. It is a
  gate in the sense that it reddens a run; it is not a merge blocker until a
  ruleset says so.

Same tool, two different consumers (security scan vs fleet learning). Removing
either loses real function — keep both.

== Secret scanning is single-sourced *in CI* — and two-tier overall

`secret-scanner.yml` runs all three estate scanners inline: `scan / gitleaks`,
`scan / rust-secrets` and `scan / shell-secrets`. An inline TruffleHog job was
removed earlier: the standards reusable it was paired with deliberately retired
TruffleHog as redundant with gitleaks, so re-adding it was duplicated work, not
extra coverage.

The three jobs are inline rather than one `uses:` of the standards
`secret-scanner-reusable.yml`, and that is deliberate. A job-level reusable call
reports `<caller job> / <called job>`, so the wrapper's three public check names
would depend on job names inside a *remote* workflow: rename one there and three
required contexts move in every generated repository. Inline jobs whose `name:`
is the context make the names this repository's own, and the whole file stays
inside `gh actions-lock`'s model — every `uses:` is a step-level action the
official generator can lock, so regenerating never leaves a dangling edge. Do
not "simplify" this back into a single wrapper call;

`metadatastician/standards` does it as a wrapper because it *owns* the reusable
and can keep `./`-local, so its own names cannot re-stale.

**That retirement is scoped to CI.** The estate runs a deliberate *two-tier*
secret defence, and the second tier is not in this directory:

[cols="1,2,3"]
|===
| Tier | Engine | Where

| CI
| gitleaks (+ rust-secrets, shell-secrets)
| `secret-scanner.yml`, three inline jobs. Runs on pull_request and on push
  to main — i.e. on what has *already reached* the remote.

| Local
| TruffleHog
| `.github/hooks/scan-secrets.sh`, called by `.github/hooks/pre-push`. Runs *before* the
  push leaves the machine, on exactly the commits being pushed.
|===

Different engines at different checkpoints — the local tier is the only one that
can stop a key before it exists on a server, where revocation, not deletion, is
the only real remedy. Ratified by the owner, 2026-09-14: *"we [run] gitleaks on
github regularly but [run] trufflehog prior to pushes using the hooks system."*

*Do not delete `.github/hooks/scan-secrets.sh` as duplication of `secret-scanner.yml`.*
It is the other half of this design, not a second copy of this half. The two
tiers also cover for each other's blind spots: the hook excludes TruffleHog's
SonarCloud detector (it matches any 40-hex string, so every SHA-pinned action
reads as a secret — measured, 24 findings on a clean clone, all of them action
pins), and gitleaks in CI catches a genuine SonarCloud token as `generic-api-key`.

== SAST tools are complementary, not redundant

* `codeql.yml` — CodeQL (matrix defaults to `actions`; every repo has workflows).
* `sonarqube.yml` — SonarCloud (shell / JS surface; see `sonar-project.properties`).
* `static-analysis-gate.yml` — pons gate on ERROR; panic-attack and patch-bridge advisory (Hypatia runs in `hypatia-scan.yml`).

Each targets a different language/surface; together they cover what no single
analyser does.

== Deed and K9 conformance come from the canon, not from this tree

`dogfood-gate.yml` validates the repo deed and the K9 contracts by calling the
two reusable lanes in hyperpolymath/standards, `deed-conformance.yml` and
`k9-conformance.yml`, at the one standards commit every `uses:` in this
directory pins. That commit supplies the linter, the validator, the K9 contract
(v1.0.0, D173) and the verdict-grid renderer, so what CI accepts is exactly
what the canon says (standards `docs/CONTRACTILE-DESCRIPTILE-VALIDATION.adoc`).

* `k9-validate` (reusable) renders the K9 grid into its job summary and the
  `k9-grid` artifact; it asks for `pull-requests: read` only. `k9-verdict`
  downloads that artifact and posts `report.md` to the pull request under
  `<!-- verdict-grid:k9 regenerated on every run -->`, one comment per PR,
  updated in place. `badges` publishes `badges/k9.json` to the
  `governance-badges` branch on eligible pushes to `main`; the README badge reads it
  through the shields endpoint; the section "The README badges are
  generated output" below states the contract that branch operates under.
* `hypatia-scan.yml` -> `verdict` job posts the Hypatia grid the same way
  (artifact `verdict-grid`, marker `<!-- verdict-grid:hypatia … -->`).

There is deliberately no second validator here: the former `k9-validate.yml`
and `deed-validate.yml` (the `k9-ecosystem` / `deed-ecosystem` actions at
`@main`) and the grep checks in `.github/hooks/validate-{k9,deed}.sh` accepted
files the contract rejects. The hooks are now thin wrappers over the same
canonical tools, run from a standards checkout (`STANDARDS_DIR`), and skip
with a notice when none is present. k9iser is retired estate-wide: contracts
are authored to `1-formats/k9/spec/K9-CONTRACT-SPEC.adoc`, never generated.

== The README badges are generated output (`governance-badges`)

Every repository minted from this template publishes one Shields-endpoint JSON
file per validation lane, on a *separate orphan branch* named
`governance-badges`:

[cols="1,1,3",options="header"]
|===
| Lane | File | Written by

| K9 conformance
| `badges/k9.json`
| `dogfood-gate.yml` -> `badges` job, on eligible pushes to `main`

|===

`README.adoc` reads that file through the shields endpoint at a URL that must
not change:

----
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/governance-badges/badges/k9.json
----

Both halves - rendering the badge and deciding whether to publish it - live in
`scripts/governance-badge.js`. The workflow only supplies the lane's result and
the lane's artifact. `tests/workflows/governance_badge_test.sh` exercises the
helper against a mock of the GitHub API and checks this directory's wiring.

=== It is generated output, not source

* `governance-badges` is an *orphan* branch. Its commits are created with
  `parents: []`, so there is *no common ancestor with `main`* - not "a little
  history", none. It is not a variant, a release branch or a staging area.
* *It must never be merged*, and there is nothing to merge: a pull request from
  it would show unrelated histories. Do not open one, do not merge one, do not
  rebase it onto `main`. Merging it would import a badges-only tree over the
  repository's real content.
* *Recent pushes are normal.* Eligible pushes to `main` republish the badge. A run
  whose badge is unchanged makes *no commit at all*, so the branch is quiet
  when the lane result is stable and moves only when the state changes.
* It is safe to delete. The next eligible push to `main` recreates it, with no parent,
  from scratch.
* It carries no workflows, no code and nothing that runs. Treat it like a
  generated site deployment, not like a branch of the repository.

=== What each colour means

[cols="1,1,1,3",options="header"]
|===
| Lane result | Badge message | Colour | Meaning

| `success`
| `success`
| brightgreen
| The lane ran, passed, and produced its artifact.

| `failure`
| `failure`
| red
| The lane ran and failed.

| `skipped`
| `skipped`
| lightgrey
| The lane did not run for this commit.

| `cancelled`
| `cancelled`
| lightgrey
| The lane started and was cancelled (superseded run, manual cancel, workflow
  concurrency).

| missing/malformed lane artifact
| `unavailable`
| lightgrey
| The lane claims success but its evidence is missing, unreadable or
  self-contradictory (for example a `success` message paired with a red
  colour). Nothing trustworthy happened, so nothing green is published.

| anything else (`timed_out`, `neutral`, `action_required`, empty, a value from
  a newer GitHub)
| `unknown`
| lightgrey
| Unrecognised. Treated as "no trustworthy result" rather than guessed at.
|===

*Grey means "this run did not produce a trustworthy success/failure result".*
It does not mean "pending", "cached" or "about to go green", and it is never a
stale green left behind by an earlier run: a workflow that runs with a skipped,
cancelled or unavailable lane *publishes grey*.

The badge reflects the *lane job's* result (`needs.k9-validate.result`), with
the lane's artifact as a *witness*: a `success` result is only believed when the
`k9-grid` artifact is present, well formed, byte-identical to the canonical
render, and itself records `success`. An artifact can never turn a failed lane
green; it can only stop a green one being published.

[NOTE]
====
*Known limit.* If the whole workflow run is cancelled, GitHub does not start
the publisher at all, so the badge keeps its previous value until the next eligible push
to `main`. No job can publish a state for a run it was not allowed to execute.
Because the run that cancels a superseded one is itself publishing, the badge
converges on the newest run's result rather than staying stuck.
====

=== Identical content produces no commit

Before writing anything, the publisher fetches the file that is currently on the
branch and compares it *byte for byte* with the badge it has just rendered.

* Identical -> it prints `unchanged`, writes no commit, and exits 0.
* Different -> it publishes with the blob sha it just read, so a concurrent
  publication is detected (HTTP 409) and re-evaluated instead of silently
  overwriting the other run's commit. Publications are also serialised by a
  per-repository `concurrency` group.
* The JSON is never re-serialised or canonicalised to make a comparison
  succeed. Key order and spacing are fixed by the renderer, and a file that
  differs only in layout *is* a difference: it gets republished.

=== Missing is not the same as broken

The publisher distinguishes the two, because treating every API error as
"missing" is how a badge pipeline quietly creates branches it should not:

[cols="1,2",options="header"]
|===
| HTTP | What happens

| `404` on the file, `404` on the ref
| The branch really is absent: create it as an orphan (`parents: []`).

| `404` on the file, `200` on the ref
| The branch exists but the file does not: add the file, no new branch.

| `404` on the file, anything else on the ref
| Unknown. Fail the run; do not create a branch.

| `401` / `403`
| Authentication or permission failure. Fail; do not write.

| `429` / `5xx`, or a network error
| Transient. Retried a bounded number of times, then fail; nothing is treated
  as missing.

| Any other status
| Fail; do not write.
|===

A malformed file that is already on the branch (not JSON, not an object, no
`schemaVersion`, no message) is *refused*, not overwritten: it did not come from
this tool, and silently replacing it would hide a hand edit. Repair or delete it
and re-run.
